note: Drops the causal 'because' and the 'particular acceptation of the term law among those jurists' clause.
replacement: We cannot see without surprise and disgust how little agreement there is among the authors who have treated this great subject. Among the more important writers there are scarcely two of the same mind. I say nothing of the ancient philosophers, who seem to have done their best to contradict one another on the most fundamental principles. The Roman jurists subjected man and the other animals indiscriminately to the same natural law, because they took that name to mean the law that nature imposes on herself rather than the law she prescribes to others. Or rather, it was because of the particular sense the term law has among those jurists, who seem on this occasion to have understood by it only the general relations nature establishes between all animated beings for their common preservation. The moderns understand by the term law merely a rule prescribed to a moral being, that is to say, to a being who is intelligent and free and is considered in his relations to other beings. They therefore confine the jurisdiction of natural law to man, as the only animal endowed with reason. But each defines this law after his own fashion, and they have founded it on such metaphysical principles that very few among us can understand them, much less discover them for ourselves. So the definitions of these learned men, which differ in everything else, agree only in this: it is impossible to understand the law of nature, and consequently to obey it, without being a very subtle casuist and a profound metaphysician. All of which is as much as to say that mankind, in establishing society, must have used a capacity that is acquired only with great difficulty, and by very few persons, even in a state of society.
